A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WARM research work. All nine pages of v1 and ten pages of v2 are readable, including equations, tables, figures, and references. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original WARM segmentation results on S3DIS and ScanNet in Tables 3–4, alongside component ablations, attention analyses, and training experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original WARM benchmark and ablation results and adds qualitative support/query segmentation comparisons in Figure 3.

M1.justification: The stated margin loss changes from a sum over query points in v1 Eq. 15 to an average in v2 Eq. 14, while its relative weighting coefficient remains fixed. The simplification loss also explicitly averages over classes. These are local objective revisions; the WARM architecture and inference remain unchanged, and the PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate indoor semantic segmentation on S3DIS and ScanNet under the same 1/2-way and 1/5-shot coverage. The added qualitative diagnostics use the existing S3DIS task and do not introduce another dataset, domain, or population.

E2.justification: Tables 3–4 add QGE and QGPA as reported comparators on both datasets across all four way/shot combinations. AttMPTI, COSeg, and FPS + min-dist. remain. This substantially broadens the primary benchmark comparison beyond v1's comparator set.

E3.justification: Table 1 changes from reporting FPS extremes for both S3DIS folds to a distribution assessment on the first fold. Section 4.2 replaces intra-/inter-class dispersion measurements with within-instance dispersion and token–feature distances. New Figure 3 also tests support self-segmentation. The principal benchmark preprocessing, episode counts, metrics, and training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The diagnostic evidence is substantially revised: Tables 1–2 rework FPS sensitivity and feature-misalignment analyses, and new Figure 3 examines COSeg and WARM failures on support and query clouds. Table 5 removes centering-only and centering-plus-coloring ablations. Attention entropy/diversity, convergence, and token-count analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Table 1 adds means and standard deviations for the described rank-aggregated FPS outcome distribution, including standard deviations of 2.41 for COSeg and 0.86 for FPS + min-dist. v1 reported only initialization extremes and cross-fold means. Both specify 1,000 FPS initializations; no increase in training runs is established.

E6.justification: Results expand through QGE/QGPA rows and new qualitative predictions, while diagnostic entries in Tables 1–2 are replaced. AttMPTI scores change in both benchmark tables; its overall S3DIS result changes from 41.26 to 37.12. Table 4 revises WARM's 1-way 1-shot mean from 39.76 to 40.13 and several FPS scores. WARM's S3DIS results remain identical. These are reported revisions, not established same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: The formal content changes locally through removal of the intra-/inter-class dispersion definitions and revisions to loss normalization and class aggregation. The componentwise cross-attention rewrite is mathematically equivalent to the earlier formulation. No theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: Both versions retain the central claims: FPS causes instability, vanilla attention suffers token–feature misalignment, whitening and coloring improve prototype construction, and WARM achieves state-of-the-art benchmark performance. The revised evidence and wording do not materially redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: Sections 4.2 and 5.2 shift the mechanism explanation from dispersion within and across support instances toward the scale discrepancy between tokens and support features. The new qualitative discussion interprets support/query predictions as evidence of better class representation and generalization. No substantive limitations discussion is added.

D1.justification: v2 explains within-episode FPS ranking and aggregation in Table 1 and specifies test-episode averaging for the dispersion analysis. Tables 3–4 change baseline provenance from official-code reproductions to Stratified Transformer results provided by the COSeg paper. Main implementation, optimizer, hardware, and training-budget disclosures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Yang et al.'s self-attention and Gumbel subset sampling paper and removes citations to Multimodality Helps, No Time to Train, and Threshold-Consistent Margin Loss. The broader research positioning remains stable. The two He et al. entries in v2 refer to the same work already cited in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and mechanism explanation receive localized rewrites, and mathematical notation is standardized. Numbered experimental subsubsections become paragraph headings, with separate quantitative and qualitative result headings. The overall seven-section narrative and substantial portions of the prose are retained.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns Tables 1–2, expands Tables 3–4 and shades WARM rows, simplifies Table 5, and adds a large qualitative comparison figure. The earlier attention-map figure becomes Figure 4 with the zero-percentile examples omitted. The pipeline figure moves and several captions expand, substantially revising the visual presentation beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: Broader baseline comparisons, explicit FPS variability reporting, and direct token–feature dispersion comparisons make the evidence more complete and easier to assess. The gain is limited by removed centering ablations and unexplained loss-normalization and score revisions. The broad ScanNet superiority wording also remains insufficiently qualified: Table 4 still places COSeg above WARM in 1-way 1-shot evaluation.
